attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own newsletter post.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps the overpromise and the one-week recognition. It leaves out the 'hero' reputational clause, but the contract adds it back. It is a firm retrospective observation.

contract.note: The plain reading is fair and ordinary: launch fell well short of Altman's own prelaunch claims, and that was broadly recognised from Aug 7 to 14, 2025. Marcus named no specific promises and gave no threshold, so the result depends on interpretation.

evidence.note: Dated in the week. Records user backlash and Altman's 'significant step' toward AGI framing. Supports only that criticism existed. It does not measure broad recognition or the size of any shortfall.
Expert criticism from Aug 8 of modest gains and a flawed demo. One selected reaction, not a representative measure.
The same roundup has favourable expert views ('progress is real'). This weakens the case for consensus but does not refute overpromising.
The Feb 2025 roadmap's commitments concern product unification, not a quantified capability promise. It is a baseline, not an outcome.

reviews.rationale: The packet shows real criticism and backlash during the week. But it has no promise-by-promise comparison showing a 'wild' shortfall, and no representative measure of broad recognition or of a reversal in Marcus's reputation. The favourable expert views cut against consensus. The evidence does not settle the claim.

attribution.note: Marcus's own parenthetical asides in his post.

semantics.note: Faithfully gives the two 'hasn't happened yet' observations and keeps the 'not yet' qualifier. It makes no forecast.

contract.note: Reading the claim as broad transformation, not any benefit at all, is fair and ordinary. Using the latest reported quarter before the post as the cutoff is reasonable. The open geographic scope is a real ambiguity.

evidence.note: US productivity rose 1.3% year over year in Q2 2025. The cycle rate is below the long-run 2.1%. There was no radical aggregate productivity increase to attribute to anything.
US real GDP fell 0.5% in Q1 and rose 3.0% in Q2, driven mainly by imports. That is ordinary variation, not a radical GDP increase.
An RCT found modest gains on simulated clinical vignettes. The authors say clinical validation is still needed, which suggests medical practice had not yet been transformed.
A lab demonstration of a GPT-4-based tool system. It shows potential, not a transformation of science, and it is not ChatGPT itself.

reviews.rationale: Official US statistics show below-trend productivity growth and ordinary GDP movement, so there was no radical aggregate increase. The scientific and medical evidence is limited to demonstrations and simulations, with authors saying real-world validation is pending. The global scope and science coverage are not exhaustive, but on the plain reading the evidence supports Marcus's 'not yet'.
